title: Anthropic Says Claude Agents Crack 23-Year-Old Black Hole Calculation
excerpt: Anthropic says a multi-agent system built on its Claude model has completed a quantum black hole transition calculation left unfinished since 2003,…
content:
Anthropic says a team of AI agents built on its Claude model has completed a quantum black hole calculation that physicists left unresolved in 2003, arriving at a result that aligns with a landmark relativity finding by Stephen Hawking and Don Page more than four decades ago.

The company said the multi-agent system determined the sign of a variable known as B, a quantity central to the problem for 23 years. The computed value, B = -0.00148 times lambda squared, is negative, indicating that a hot, soup-like state of particles collapses into a black hole abruptly rather than gradually as temperature rises.

That outcome matches what Hawking and Page described in 1983. The two physicists studied a hypothetical closed universe shaped like a cosmic ball from which energy cannot escape and found that a black hole takes over at a critical temperature. What remained missing was the corresponding quantum picture, where conventional notions of spacetime break down.

The problem sits at the fault line between general relativity, which governs the very large, and quantum mechanics, which governs the very small. Black holes involve both scales, and the two frameworks do not always appear to agree. Hawking's own work suggested that evaporating black holes might destroy information, while quantum mechanics holds that information must be preserved. The new calculation addresses the transition itself, not the separate and still-open question of information loss.

Physicists established in 2003 that the quantum version of the temperature problem reduces to the sign of B. The technique, called Landau analysis, can be pictured as a ball resting at the bottom of a valley, with one side representing the initial particle state and the other a black hole. As temperature climbs, the landscape shifts. A positive B would let the ball roll gradually away from the soup state; a negative B opens a second valley that deepens until the ball switches sides.

Getting there required accounting for the many ways quantum particles can interact, each represented by a Feynman diagram that becomes a piece of the overall calculation. A simplified version of the problem needed 14 three-loop diagrams, and 13 of them produced infinity. The pieces had to be combined with the correct corrections for those infinities to cancel, a bookkeeping task no one had finished in more than two decades. The full problem, according to Anthropic, involves many thousands of diagrams.

According to the company, several copies of Claude operated as a small research team, each deriving portions of the calculation independently and cross-checking the mathematics against known results. The agents divided the work into smaller tasks and wrote programs to solve them.

The result applies to a simplified theoretical universe rather than our own and does not amount to a theory of quantum gravity. The more instructive element may be the method: splitting a large, error-sensitive computation into pieces and having agents verify one another's output is a workflow that could transfer to other problems where a single mistake ruins the answer.

The claim lands amid a broader push by AI developers into frontier mathematics. Anthropic has previously publicized work in which its models advanced partial results on the Riemann hypothesis, the 167-year-old conjecture carrying a $1 million prize. In that episode, the company said a model raised the proven lower bound for the proportion of nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function lying on the critical line to 67.2% from 41.6%, a result later analyzed and verified by its own mathematicians.

That earlier work drew attention partly because the verification was carried out internally. The black hole calculation faces a similar test: the value of B and the cancellation of 13 infinities are reported by the company, and independent physicists would need to reproduce the derivation before the result enters the literature.

For researchers tracking AI's role in science, the significance is less the specific number than the division of labor it demonstrates. A calculation that defeated human patience for 23 years was broken into modular pieces, solved by programs written on the fly, and checked against benchmarks already established. Whether that approach scales to problems without known answers to check against remains the open question.
